contexts.title: The competition rule and its definition of sex
contexts.html: The bill makes it a violation of Title IX for a school or college that receives federal money and “operates, sponsors, or facilitates athletic programs or activities to permit a person whose sex is male to participate in an athletic program or activity that is designated for women or girls.” [1] For this rule, “sex shall be recognized based solely on a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth.” [1]

source_refs.quote: operates, sponsors, or facilitates athletic programs or activities to permit a person whose sex is male to participate in an athletic program or activity that is designated for women or girls.
sex shall be recognized based solely on a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth.

contexts.title: The training and practice exception
contexts.html: A covered school may still let males train or practice with a women’s or girls’ team “so long as no female is deprived of a roster spot on a team or sport, opportunity to participate in a practice or competition, scholarship, admission to an educational institution, or any other benefit that accompanies participating in the athletic program or activity.” [1] The exception allows practice only. It does not allow competition in that program.

source_refs.quote: so long as no female is deprived of a roster spot on a team or sport, opportunity to participate in a practice or competition, scholarship, admission to an educational institution, or any other benefit that accompanies participating in the athletic program or activity.
The exception does not permit competition in that program.

contexts.title: Activities that depend on being on a team
contexts.html: The rule’s term for sports “includes, but is not limited to, all programs or activities that are provided conditional upon participation with any athletic team.” [1] Conditional upon participation means open only to people on the team.

contexts.title: The law in force on January 14, 2025
contexts.html:
The comparison is with the law in force on January 14, 2025. The Congressional Research Service (CRS) says: “Neither the statute nor the regulations currently address how Title IX applies to transgender athletes.” [1] Older rules allowed separate teams: “Long-standing Title IX regulations permit separation of the sexes in school sports programs provided schools offer equal athletic opportunities.” [2]

Practice differed by place. Some places let transgender students compete “with no particular requirements or restrictions.” [3] College sports used testosterone limits: “Between January 19, 2022, and February 6, 2025, the NCAA called for the participation of transgender athletes to be regulated on a sport-by-sport basis.” [4] Other states had laws “requiring student-athletes to participate on teams according to their sex assigned at birth.” [3]

contexts.title: The B.P.J. ruling in force on the comparison date
contexts.html: On January 14, 2025, a federal appeals court ruling was in force in the states that court covers. The court wrote: “We do not hold that government officials are forbidden from creating separate sports teams for boys and girls” [3].

blocks.html: After the comparison date, on June 30, 2026, the Supreme Court reversed the Fourth Circuit’s B.P.J. judgment and the Ninth Circuit’s Hecox judgment and sent both back to the lower courts. It held that Title IX and the Equal Protection Clause allow states to keep female sports teams defined by biological sex, without an exception for students who have taken puberty blockers or hormones. The decision permits such state rules. It does not impose a nationwide requirement like H.R.28. It calls participation a debated policy question and describes the science of retained advantage as subject to ongoing debate. A word search of the opinion found no discussion of sex-verification procedures or examinations.

blocks.html: A 2026 systematic review in the British Journal of Sports Medicine (52 studies) reports transgender women and other women as similar on average in relative lean mass, upper-body and lower-body strength and maximal oxygen use. The statistical ranges for those comparisons include no difference, and certainty is rated low or very low. The review concludes that transgender women have higher lean mass with comparable fitness, and says: “Current evidence is mostly low certainty and has heterogenous quality but does not support theories of inherent athletic advantages for transgender women over cisgender.” [4] A later correction removed three studies, added one and left the main conclusions unchanged. These are averages for body composition and fitness, with no result by sport for absolute mass, speed, collisions or injuries. Only the abstract and correction notice were available, so the full methods were not checked. The review came after the comparison date but before the evidence cutoff.

The evidence does not settle whether transgender women who train and compete keep the speed and power advantage this claim needs. The same review says that “athletic performance in transgender people who engage in training and competition, remain unknown.” [5] It also says: “The levels of physical activity of the transwomen compared with cisgender women in the studies were not reported.” [5] A 2024 study measured athletes at one point in time and found mixed results: transgender women athletes had “higher absolute handgrip strength” [6] but “lower relative jump height” [6], which takes body weight into account. nodes.title: Limited places and scholarships kept for girls
nodes.claim_html: Where team places, chances to practice or compete, or athletic scholarships are limited, the bill would keep some of them for female athletes that would otherwise go to competitors it classifies as male.

nodes.title: Sport-linked environmental activity kept
nodes.claim_html: Some female athletes who keep a place, practice time or scholarship because of the bill would thereby keep sport-linked environmental activity: team cleanups and recycling projects, time rowing on waters where they see and remove pollution, or scholarship support for environmental study. Any one of these is enough.

nodes.title: Nature: environmental activity kept
nodes.claim_html: Cleanups, recycling projects, removing litter from the water and research on preventing water pollution are ways of caring for nature and defending it from pollution. Keeping female athletes’ access to any one of them serves those goals.

nodes.title: Team environmental activity lost by excluded students
nodes.claim_html: Some students the bill excludes from women’s teams would lose team-based ways to care for nature: outdoor competition that can build concern for the environment, or team posts that lead environmental work, such as a women’s team’s sustainability captain. Either is enough.

nodes.title: Nature: team environmental activity lost
nodes.claim_html: Outdoor competition that builds care for nature, and team posts that organize cleanups and conservation work, are ways of caring for nature and taking part in defending it. Closing either to excluded students works against those goals.

nodes.title: Retained strength advantage
nodes.claim_html: In events that depend on speed and power, transgender women who went through male puberty keep a strength advantage over other women even after hormone treatment, so the bill would keep that advantage out of covered female competition.

nodes.title: Concern: a fair chance at wins and recognition
nodes.claim_html: Keeping a retained strength advantage out of female competition gives women a real chance to earn wins and recognition. That serves equal opportunity and just treatment.

nodes.title: Concern: places and their benefits kept for girls
nodes.claim_html: Keeping limited places and sports money for girls keeps their chances at the education and leadership benefits those places bring. That serves equal opportunities in life.

nodes.title: Lower collision risk in women’s contact sports
nodes.claim_html: In covered women’s contact competition, such as rugby, the bill would remove matchups with athletes who went through male puberty and kept differences in size, speed and force after lowering testosterone. Where hormone-based rules had allowed those matchups, this would lower the added risk of collision injury for smaller players.

nodes.title: Personal Security: lower collision risk
nodes.claim_html: Lower risk of collision injury in an ordinary way to exercise serves avoiding injury and danger.

nodes.title: Concern: protecting smaller players
nodes.claim_html: Protecting smaller players from collision forces they are less able to withstand protects the physically vulnerable, including girls one does not know.

nodes.title: Concern: games not given up over safety fears
nodes.claim_html: Where a girls’ team would give up games because of safety concerns about an opponent the bill classifies as male, removing that matchup keeps the team’s games. That protects girls whose chance to play would otherwise be lost.

nodes.title: Concern: team learning and benefits closed to excluded students
nodes.claim_html: Barring transgender and nonbinary students the bill classifies as male from girls’ and women’s teams, and from activities tied to those teams, closes a route to learning, scholarships and admission that other students keep. Concern for equal opportunity includes these students.

nodes.title: Concern: individual protection replaced by automatic exclusion
nodes.claim_html: On the comparison date, the law in one federal circuit protected an individual girl whom exclusion treated worse than comparable students. Replacing that protection with a duty to exclude, whatever a student’s circumstances, conflicts with treating everyone justly.

nodes.title: Tolerance: a legal route to inclusion closed
nodes.claim_html: Including a classmate despite disagreement about that classmate’s gender, and hearing the student’s situation before ruling the student out, are ways of accepting people who differ. The bill would close that route, which the law then in force protected in some cases, and the team-linked chances to know one another.

nodes.title: Tolerance: girls whose beliefs rule out the matchup
nodes.claim_html: Accepting people despite disagreement includes accepting girls whose religious or other beliefs differ from one’s own. Removing the matchup that forces them to choose between their belief and playing keeps a way for them to play.

nodes.title: Girls with intersex variations pushed out or deterred
nodes.claim_html: The bill’s birth-based test would leave some girls born with intersex variations unsure whether they may play, and would push some of them out of girls’ sports or discourage them from playing.

nodes.title: Concern: girls with intersex variations
nodes.claim_html: Uncertain eligibility, and being pushed out of girls’ sports, take away chances that other girls keep. Concern for equal opportunity includes girls born with intersex variations.

nodes.title: Tolerance: girls with intersex variations
nodes.claim_html: Accepting all kinds of people includes accepting people born with different bodies. Exposing girls to exclusion because their bodies do not fit a simple birth-based test conflicts with that acceptance.

nodes.title: Exclusion isolates and stigmatizes
nodes.claim_html: Barring students the bill classifies as male from girls’ and women’s teams would isolate and stigmatize some transgender, nonbinary and intersex students.

nodes.title: Concern: support removed and stigma added for vulnerable students
nodes.claim_html: Students who already face more violence, distress and isolation need protection. Taking away a source of support while adding stigma burdens them, which conflicts with protecting the vulnerable.

nodes.title: Tolerance: classmates marked as outsiders
nodes.claim_html: Accepting and understanding people who differ conflicts with treatment that marks some classmates as outsiders and adds stigma against them.

nodes.title: Stigma harms mental health beyond athletes
nodes.claim_html: The stigma of this exclusion would worsen the mental health of some students, including some transgender students who do not play sports, by weakening the supportive school ties that protect it.

nodes.title: Personal Security: mental health in everyday school life
nodes.claim_html: Protecting mental health in everyday school life is part of protecting health.

nodes.title: Excluded students leave sport
nodes.claim_html: Some transgender students the bill excludes from girls’ and women’s teams would stop playing school sports rather than play on a team based on their sex at birth.

nodes.title: Fear deters eligible girls
nodes.claim_html: Fear of accusations, intrusive questions or checks would discourage some girls whom the bill still allows to play from taking part in sports.

nodes.title: Concern: eligible girls discouraged from playing
nodes.claim_html: When fear of accusations or humiliating checks makes it harder for eligible girls to play, especially girls who do not fit stereotypes, their chances in life become less equal.

nodes.title: Health lost by students who stop playing
nodes.claim_html: Some students who stop playing because of the bill, whether excluded from girls’ teams or discouraged by fear, would lose exercise, supportive team relationships or sports-linked checkups that protect their physical or mental health. The route through excluded students needs the claim that some leave sport; the route through discouraged girls needs the claim about fear.

nodes.title: Personal Security: exercise and health support lost
nodes.claim_html: Losing exercise, supportive relationships and checkups works against avoiding disease and protecting health.

nodes.title: Girls keep exercise and its health benefits
nodes.claim_html: Some girls who keep a team place or practice chance because of the bill, and have no other place to play, would keep exercise and its physical and mental health benefits that they would otherwise lose.

nodes.title: Personal Security: girls’ exercise kept
nodes.claim_html: Keeping a way to exercise, with its physical and mental health benefits, serves protecting health and avoiding disease.

nodes.title: Concern: an equal chance at the health benefits of sport
nodes.claim_html: Keeping girls’ chance at the health benefits of team sport serves equal opportunities in life.

nodes.title: Kept places give practice in acceptance
nodes.claim_html: Girls who keep team places because of the bill would keep a setting where they learn to understand and accept teammates who differ from them.

nodes.title: Tolerance: practice in accepting teammates
nodes.claim_html: Learning to listen to, understand and accept teammates who differ is practice in tolerance. Keeping girls’ chances to practice those habits serves that value.

nodes.title: Less unwanted shared undressing
nodes.claim_html: The bill would keep some athletes it classifies as male out of changing areas used by women’s and girls’ teams, reducing unwanted shared undressing. This could happen because changing tied to team membership is itself a covered activity, or because athletes excluded from female competition would no longer use its changing area. Either is enough.

nodes.title: Personal Security: privacy when changing
nodes.claim_html: Undressing with others against one’s wishes can damage a sense of security. Privacy in intimate settings supports feeling personally safe and secure.

nodes.title: Intrusive inquiries without bodily exams
nodes.claim_html: Enforcing the bill in schools that had included transgender girls would bring some intrusive inquiries into students’ records, private history or bodies, like the Florida investigation, even without bodily examinations.

nodes.title: Pressure for invasive bodily checks
nodes.claim_html: Because H.R.28 sets a biological test and no method for checking it, schools would come under pressure to use invasive bodily checks. Those checks would expose girls to humiliation, distress or sexual abuse.

nodes.title: Concern: children’s privacy, dignity and bodily safety
nodes.claim_html: Intrusive inquiries into a child’s private history, with exposure, humiliation and disrupted schooling, would harm vulnerable children; so would humiliating bodily checks with a risk of abuse. Either consequence alone gives a reason against the rule. Inquiries need the claim about inquiries; checks need the claim about bodily checks.

nodes.title: Personal Security: invasive checks and their trauma
nodes.claim_html: Bodily intrusion, the risk of sexual abuse and the distress these checks cause in an ordinary school activity work against being safe, secure and healthy.

nodes.title: Tradition: religious modesty and intimate privacy
nodes.claim_html: Intimate questions about whether teammates saw a girl undressed would conflict with inherited religious practices of modesty and intimate privacy; so would invasive checks. Either alone gives a reason against the rule. Questions need the claim about inquiries; checks need the claim about bodily checks.

nodes.title: More appearance-based accusations
nodes.claim_html: Making birth sex decide eligibility in covered schools nationwide would bring more accusations, based on a girl’s body, appearance or performance, that she was born male. Some of these would bring investigations, harassment or threats, including against girls who are not transgender.

nodes.title: Concern: harassment for appearance
nodes.claim_html: Harassment and threats aimed at girls for how they look, falling especially on girls who do not fit race or gender stereotypes, conflict with treating everyone justly and protecting vulnerable children.

nodes.title: Tolerance: differences turned into grounds for suspicion
nodes.claim_html: Tolerance toward different people conflicts with rules that turn differences in bodies, appearance and gender expression into reasons for suspicion, challenges to eligibility and harassment.

nodes.title: Personal Security: threats against accused girls
nodes.claim_html: Threats against girls, including girls who are not transgender, and against their families make accusations a safety concern in ordinary school sports.

nodes.title: Accusations intimidate wider communities
nodes.claim_html: These accusations and threats would frighten wider school communities, not only the girls accused.

nodes.title: Societal Security: intimidation of communities
nodes.claim_html: Protecting citizens and their communities from threats is part of a secure country with a state that can defend its citizens.

nodes.title: Less protection against youth drug use and violence
nodes.claim_html: By keeping some students out of school sports, or by weakening their school ties, the bill would reduce sport’s protection against youth drug use or violence, making communities somewhat less safe. This can come through excluded students who leave sport, girls with intersex variations who are pushed out, or the stigma of exclusion. Any one is enough.

nodes.title: Societal Security: safer communities
nodes.claim_html: Protection against youth drug use and violence, and stronger community ties, help the country protect its people and stay secure and stable.

nodes.title: Federal money for other students put at risk
nodes.claim_html: Some covered schools would keep including transgender girls and so put federal money for the affected program at risk, which could harm other students that money serves.

nodes.title: Concern: other students’ educational money at risk
nodes.claim_html: Federal education money supports many students’ opportunities. Making inclusion grounds for withdrawing it puts other students’ equal opportunities at risk.

nodes.title: Larger, stronger and faster opponents for girls moved to boys’ teams
nodes.claim_html: Some girls the bill excludes who have not gone through male puberty, such as girls who took puberty-blocking treatment, would compete against boys who are larger, stronger and faster than them if they kept competing on a sex-separated school team by joining a boys’ team.

nodes.title: Concern: an unequal contest moved onto vulnerable girls
nodes.claim_html: For these girls, the remaining way to keep competing on a sex-separated team is a contest against larger, stronger and faster opponents. Protecting vulnerable students from an unfair contest gives a reason against moving that disadvantage onto them.

nodes.title: Added physical danger in some sports
nodes.claim_html: In some sports, competing against those larger, stronger and faster boys would expose some of these girls to added physical danger.

nodes.title: Concern: physical danger moved onto vulnerable girls
nodes.claim_html: For girls who want to keep competing on a sex-separated team, the remaining choice brings added physical danger in those sports. Protecting vulnerable students gives a reason against moving that risk onto them.

nodes.title: Tradition: an inherited understanding of sex in school sports
nodes.claim_html: Making a public sports rule follow the inherited Christian understanding of sex as male and female, which parents are taught to pass down, maintains that traditional way of thinking.

nodes.title: Tradition: separate female competition
nodes.claim_html: Reserving female competition and its titles for female athletes preserves an established form of women’s sports. Honoring a culture’s established practices supports keeping it.

nodes.title: Tradition: family and local authority over upbringing
nodes.claim_html: The tradition teaches that parents, and smaller groups such as schools and communities, are responsible for children’s upbringing. A federal rule that removes their choice to approve a child’s participation takes a decision away from them.
